idiom_name: ServiceBuilder with timeout / concurrency-limit / trace layers
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, but tower turns the pattern into a compositional, typed middleware stack: every service is a Service, and a Layer wraps one service in another, so timeouts, concurrency limits, retries, rate limits, load balancing and tracing are added by composing layers over an unchanged service, with ServiceExt combinators (map_request, map_response, oneshot) for ad-hoc control. The stack stays generic - nothing is boxed or dynamically dispatched unless the type is deliberately erased - and the same abstraction covers clients and servers, HTTP and gRPC.
pitfalls: Cloning a tower Service is meant to hand out another handle to the same service: a proxy that clones stateful innards per call can duplicate limiters, metrics or connections.
poll_ready must be forwarded (or deliberately overridden): a layer that always reports ready removes the backpressure the inner service depends on and can overload it.
Layer order carries semantics: a timeout outside a retry bounds the total budget, inside it bounds each attempt; choose and document the order.

variants.name: Hand-written struct implementing the service trait
variants.idiom_name: struct holding the service, implementing the same trait
variants.implementation_notes: For a plain trait (not a tower Service) the proxy is a struct holding the inner service that implements the same trait and forwards each method with policy applied inline; ownership makes the delegation explicit, and the compiler rejects any member the proxy fails to forward. Choose this form for synchronous or non-async service traits, or when a tower stack would be over-engineering, and prefer a generic parameter over trait objects so calls stay monomorphised.
pitfalls: The proxy must mirror the trait's associated types and generic bounds exactly; drift surfaces as a compile error at the call site, which makes it tempting to blame the caller.
Holding the service by value makes the proxy single-owner: share it with Arc (or borrow it) when several call sites need one service, and mind Send/Sync bounds in async code.
A generic proxy monomorphises per service type, so a boxed dyn ServiceApi at the boundary erases the type and reintroduces dynamic dispatch cost.
